speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members of this house learned yesterday afternoon, I am sure with sorrow, of the death at his home at St. Constant, Quebec, of Mr. Roch Lanctot, member for Laprairie-Napier-ville. Mr. Lanctot had been in ill health for [Mr Duff.]
some time past; indeed, he was unable to be present at all during this session of parliament and was absent during the latter part of the last session. His death therefore, was not unexpected. At the same time, I am sure it will bring a feeling of sadness to the hearts of all present to realize that we shall not again see within this chamber or about the corridors of parliament, his familiar figure.
Mr. Lanctot was in his sixty-fourth year. In years of representation in parliament he was one of the oldest members. He came into the House of Commons after the general elections of 1904 and was again returned in the elections of 1908, 1911, 1917, 1921, 1925 and 1926, a continuous service, as a member of parliament, of some twenty-five years. During the whole of that time Mr. Lanctot was very faithful in the discharge of his duties as a member, in attendance upon the sittings and work of the house and in representing in parliament the interests of his constituents and, in particular, the interests of the agricultural classes with which he was specially identified. It was characteristic of his concern for ,the people and their welfare that, in addition to being a member of parliament he should have continued to interest himself in municipal affairs. He was, 'at the time of his death, mayor of the parish in which he lived.
Mr. Lanctot was a true son of the soil. He was born in the country; he came to Ottawa for his early education, but thereafter returned to the farm and devoted himself to rural pursuits. He was not only a son of the soil but a lover of the soil and was true to the soil. Had he lived in France he would have been spoken of as a peasant proprietor; had he lived in Great Britain he would have been referred to as one of the yeomen of the country, the class of men who in both these lands are the backbone of the nation, and who are known throughout the world as the salt of the earth. In Canada he brought to the rural life of our country what was best in the rural life of these older countries, with which through blood or birth he was associated. A true representation of the type of man of which Mr. Lanctot was an outstanding example is given, it seems to me, by Gray, in his Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard:
Some village Hampden, that, with dauntless breast,
The little tyrant of his fields withstood,
Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest,
Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood.

The late Mr. Lanctot
Mr. Lanctot had many of .the characteristics of a Hampden. He was a man of sturdy independence and of sterling integrity; one who would not submit to arbitrary measures; who was fearless and courageous; prepared to stand alone for a principle in which he believed. He had many of the qualities of a Milton. He possessed a deep religious conviction, a strong faith. He was a lover of nature and there was about him, in his love of the simple and beautiful things of life, in his broad human sympathies and great friendliness of heart, not a little of the poet and the philosopher. He had, too, many of the attributes of a Cromwell. He was one who had a hatred of caste and of class; he was a great believer in the commonwealth, the commonweal, and at all times and on all occasions he stood for the rights of the people. This is the man who has passed away from our midst.
Speaking more particularly of the party to which he belonged, may I say that we had in him one of the firmest of upholders of Liberal principles. He was an intimate friend and strong supporter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier during the time that Sir Wilfrid was the leader of the Liberal party. In the ten years that it has been my privilege to be in the leadership of the party, he accorded to me a like friendship and an equally loyal support. Personally I feel his death very deeply. I am sure that feeling is shared in equal measure by all who sit on this side of the house, and I believe it is felt in great measure by all members of parliament, irrespective of party.
May I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to convey to his widow the sympathy of this house in her great bereavement. The 'house I am sure will feel sympathy for the constituency as well, the constituency which has lost a member who has represented it continuously and faithfully for so long a period of time. Perhaps nothing more worthy could be expressed of his name and his fame than to say he was as much respected and beloved by members in this house of parliament as he was honoured by the constituency which over a quarter of a century gave him an unbroken confidence.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I, on behalf of those who are associated with me to your left as well as on my own, express my great sympathy with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his party in the loss they have sustained by the death of a beloved colleague? Mr. Lanctot possessed those qualities that endeared him greatly to those with whom he was associated, and I can
readily understand the reason for the moving sentences with which the Prime Minister expressed the sense of the loss sustained by him and his party in the passing of Mr. Lanctot. It was my privilege to know Mr. Lanctot for many years. I did not know him nearly so intimately as the Prime Minister and his colleagues did, but I knew enough of him to realize something of his sturdy character, sterling qualities and the devotion he gave to the service of his country. It may wel be said that he was desirous at all times of adding to his store of knowledge. Perhaps some members of the house will recall a speech that he made on one occasion in which he indicated that he came here a young man desirous of learning and that he had learned much by his experience in this house.
He was a very devout man and a son of his church in the true sense. I think from a brief conversation I had with him that he would describe himself as a Canadian with all that it involves-a son of the soil who loved his native province with a devotion that was sometimes touching, one who loved the soil as only perhaps a Canadian can who is proud of his country, proud of its achievements, and looks forward to its future with great hope.
He was a man of real integrity of character, and his views were not easily disturbed once he had arrived at a conclusion. While my hon. friend the Prime Minister described him as a very strong supporter of his party, I am bound to say that in the discussions that I have had with him, not less than in some of his public utterances, there was a strong indication that while his views were generally in accord with those of the Prime Minister, he held very conservative principles and I think most of those who knew him well will agree that that was so.
I am glad to associate myself with the Prime Minister in the sympathy that he has expressed for Mr. Lanctot's family, who have lost a loving and devoted husband and a father whose memory will be cherished with pride and satisfaction. He has rendered service to his country. His character and his achievements will serve as an example to those who come after him in the community in which he lived. His love of his country was manifested in every possible way in which it could be done within the sphere of his influence. The quotation which the Prime Minister has made from the poet Gray I would supplement with this other stanza:
No farther seek his merits to disclose,
Or draw his frailties from their dread abode,
(There they alike in trembling hope repose,)
The bosom of his Father and his God.
Business o] the House

Mr. Speaker, it was with regret that we heard of the death of Mr. Lanctot late yesterday afternoon. Mr. Lanctot was for many years a very very faithful member of this house and I am sure that he served his constituency well. We in this corner of the house desire to associate ourselves with the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in paying tribute to the memory of the late Mr. Lanctot, and we also wish to express our sympathy to his widow and his family.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	May I be allowed to voice my deep
appreciation of the work of Mr. Lanctot, of his very attractive qualities and of his sterling worth? He had a charming personality. He had two things in common. He had a deep love of the people who live on the land and till the soil, and he was extremely interested in the peace of the world. With me he believed that if we continued to train our boys and girls in military methods, we would continue to use military methods. For all of these reasons I want personally to associate myself with the three members who have spoken in appreciation of the work which Mr. Lanctot did for the coming generations in this country.

The motion on the order
paper with respect to Saturday sittings in order to be moved at this time will require the unanimous consent of the house. Before asking for that, may I say that in now presenting the motion I am doing so with a view to hearing hon. members express their views and feelings on the wisdom of sitting to-morrow. I recognize that we have had a pretty hoit week so far as the temperature is concerned, and a good many I imagine are feeling its fatigue and exhaustion, none more so than the members of the administration. However, we are quite prepared to sit to-morrow and continue with the work of the house with a view to hastening the termination of the session if such appears to be the wish of hon. members.
May I say in regard to sitting on Monday that last year, as I recollect it, the house sat on the King's birthday but adjourned during the afternoon in order that hon. members might attend the garden party given by Their Excellencies in honour of His Majesty's birthday. We had thought of following a similar

procedure this year but again, if Mr. Speaker would permit it, I would like to have an expression of the views of the house and the government -will seek to be guided in its final decision in the matter by what appears to be the general view.

I will put the motion. It is moved by the Prime Minister:
That on Saturday, the first day of June, 1929, and every Saturday thereafter until the end of the session, the house shall meet at eleven o'clock in the forenoon and the order of business and procedure shall be the same as on Fridays.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
It is undoubted, Mr. Speaker,
that the notice of motion now given by the Prime Minister has only become necessary because it was found that the first motion was not sufficiently 'broad to cover the matter, for it was originally intended to deal with to-morrow as well as every succeeding Saturday until the house prorogued.
I think we are all desirous of doing our best to expedite the business of parliament. We certainly should not sit for three sittings to-morrow. Whether or not we should sit until six o'clock to-morrow is a matter in respect to which those who sit to the left of the Speaker are entirely in the hands of the majority of the house. If the majority of the house so desire, we certainly are willing to expedite business by sitting.
With respect to Monday, I think the course suggested by the Prime Minister is one that might well be followed. We can have a sitting in the morning, adjourn for the afternoon, and sit in the evening from eight until eleven. I see no reason why that should not be done, and those associated with me are quite willing to assist in carrying out that idea.

So far as the sittings on Monday are concerned, it is agreeable to us to sit in the morning and in the evening, as the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition suggest, leaving the afternoon free for those who desire to attend the garden party. But to sitting on Saturdays we have very strong objection. We have been having three sittings every day all week, and we have other business in our offices that we must attend .to, and with three sittings a day we have not very much opportunity to take care of that business that our constituents expect us to take care of. Saturday is the only day we have left in which to do that business.
I want to draw the attention of the house to a very important point. The members from the maritimes and we from the west.

Mixing of Wheat
have to sit here week in and week out. We cannot go home on Friday night and come back on Monday night like most of the members from Ontario and Quebec. It is the practice of this house not to transact important business on Friday or Monday; no important votes are ever taken on a Friday or a Monday. The consequence is that we who have to sit here all week can only mill around, if I may use that expression, until the other members come back. We get tired of this kind of business. We do not think it is fair. Then when we come to the end of the session there is a great rush, against which we have always protested. As far as we are concerned we will not consent to sitting on any Saturday during the rest of this session. I understand that this motion is not in order, Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as it was not placed on the order paper in time. Therefore I raise objection against the passing of the motion.

If objection is raised, I
must declare that it is valid, because the motion is out of order unless there is unanimous consent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct the attention of the ministry, and especially the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mir. Malcolm) to a most mischievous and inaccurate statement which appears in the morning newspapers. This mischievous and inaccurate statement is the report of some publication in London, England. The diplomatic correspondent of the London Morning Post is reported by Mr. Lukin Johnston of the Southam Press as having said:
One aspect of American activity in Canada requires close attention and that is in the mixing of low grade American wheat with
Canadian, and exporting it as Canadian. This must affect, in a measure, the Canadian market abroad.
As that statement, Mr. Speaker, is inaccurate, is mischievous and calculated to do irreparable harm to our wheat industry overseas, I ask that the Minister of Trade and Commerce take the necessary steps to correct it.

speakeroldname: Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CORRECTION OP INACCURATE STATEMENT BY CORRESPONDENT OF LONDON NEWSPAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to thank my hon. friend the member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), for calling the attention of parliament to this statement which, as he says, is entirely inaccurate. Neither from Montreal, Halifax, St. John or Vancouver is a Canadian western certificate issued on anything but all-Canadian wheat, and how the impression has gone abroad as to the mixing of Canadian and American spring wheats in Montreal I do not know. But I think at this time it might just as well be stated clearly to the house that there is an admixture of Canadian and American durum wheat, but that wheat does not go out under a Canadian western certificate. The wheat that is mixed at Montreal is what is known as macaroni wheat or durum wheat Those wheats of both Canadian and American origin are sold out of American seaboard ports and out of Canadian ports on what is known as an open or seaboard certificate, which does mot give the country of origin, either passing through an American port or a Canadian port. The statement that they are low-grades or high-grades as of either country is incorrect. Durum wheats are used in the macaroni trade in Europe, and the buyers know exactly what they are getting. In many instances the admixture may consist of a high-grade American durum and a low-grade Canadian durum. In other instances it may be that the grade of Canadian durum is higher than the grade of American durum, and I think it is with regard to this admixture which is sold on an open or seaboard certificate in both countries that the impression mentioned has been created. But may I repeat again, that all wheat passing through Canadian ports on Canadian certificates is entirely of Canadian origin, and that the statement referred to by my hon. friend, and contained in The Citizen this morning, is incorrect.

In answer to my hon. friend I may say that I have absolutely no doubt that if the attention of the government were drawn to such a situation the governor in council would see *to it that no such Monday would be chosen as election day, so any inconvenience such as that indicated by my hon. friend certainly would' be overcome.
I might point out that these fasts and feasts may occur on Mondays or Tuesdays; they are not definitely fixed.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4-Polling day to be half holiday.

Yesterday I asked that this
section stand in order to consider the question of the half holiday which, under the present bill, would be observed all over Canada. As I pointed out then, under the old bill employees were given two hours off with pay, but under this bill they would not be paid for this half holiday. In other words, they are to be denied certain rights they previously enjoyed, and I did feel that this was a retrograde step. I would be very much in favour of a half holiday, of course, if the employees received pay for that time off, but not otherwise. I do not think it was the intention of the committee to penalize employees in this way if they desired to exercise their franchise.
Yesterday I was under the impression that just before the one o'clock adjournment an amendment had been moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson), but on looking up Hansard I find that such was not the case. However, I see that the chairman of the committee accepted the suggestion on behalf of the government, for which I am very grateful.
No,

My hon. friend shakes his
head; I will quote what he said:
I understand that the government have no objection to accepting this amendment-
Such being the case, I do not see now why the chairman of that committee should shake his head and object to the statement I am making. I think most members of the house [DOT]will remember that just before one o'clock yesterday the hon. member did make the statement as reported in Hansard.

If I may just interrupt, I
may have made the statement but I have no recollection of doing so. I really did not intend to say that.

I will attribute it to the
heat, but I presume that the Hansard reporter took down exactly what the hon. member said, even though he does not remember making the statement.

I did not mean to Say it;
I think my hon. friend will permit me to

Dominion Elections Act
make that correction. I am quite clear in my own mind that I did not mean to attempt to bind the government, over which I have no power or influence, or even to bind myself, over whom I am presumed to have some influence.

I must say that the hon.
gentleman is very modest. However, Mr. Chairman, I intend to move an amendment to section 4 as follows:
That section 14 of the Dominion Elections Act be substituted for section 4 in the present bill, Ho. 313. except that the word "three'' shall be substituted in the second line for the word "two".
The effect of this amendment, which I hope will receive the support of the government, will be to give men and women Who are employed in factories and elsewhere three hours off on election day without any deduction from their pay.
Why not make the motion in the exact terms in which you wish it adopted?

I think that is what I have
done; I think this covers exactly what I wish. As a matter of fact I thought this amendment had been moved yesterday; only a few moments ago I learned that this was not the case, so I drafted this amendment hurriedly to cover the point. The only change from the old act I am asking is that the word "three" be substituted for the word "two," which would make the section read as follows:
Every employer shall, on polling day, allow every elector in his employ at least three additional hours other than the noon hour-
I would suggest that in as much as section 4 had been adopted-
No, it has not been adopted; if that had been the case I could not have made this amendment.
You are substituting the old section and inserting the word "three" instead of two."

Yes. It has been stated that this parliament has no power to legislate along these lines. I cannot say as to that, but nevertheless I do know that in past years the large employers of labour in this country have carried out the spirit of the act and have given to their employees the two hours provided for in the old elections act, which we are now amending. I know what has happened in the large shops out west; on election day they closed down at 3 o'clock m the afternoon, so the employees were given 78594-1961
two hours off with pay. I beiieve the same practice has been followed by other companies employing large numbers of men and women. Under this bill now before us a half holiday is declared on election day; that is something I would like to see carried out, and I believe the wording of my amendment is in accordance with the intentions of the committee. The large employers of labour usually keep open from 8 to 12, and then from 1 o'clock in the afternoon. They would probably work from 8 o'clock in the morning until 1 o'clock in the afternoon under this arrangement, and I think every large employer of labour in the Dominion would follow that practice. I am not so much concerned with the question of the powers which we have under the British North America Act, because it strikes me most forcibly that whenever anything comes up which concerns the working people of this country the British North America Act is always brought forward to their disadvantage. Under the old act the employees were given two hours and when we try to extend that by one hour we aTe told that we have not the power to do so. It was done in the past, the employers of labour carried out the spirit of the enactment of parliament and I feel quite satisfied that if this amendment is adopted they will carry out the spirit of the amendment in the same way as they carried out the provisions of the Dominion Election Act.

I have a copy of Hansard
before me and I find that the hon. member is quite correct; I did intimate that the government seemed to be willing to accept that suggestion, but I said also that as chairman of the committee I wished to dissociate myself from it. May I repeat briefly my reason for taking that stand; it is quite true that there are provisions in the act whereby an employee may, for a period of two hours, absent himself from his work for the purpose of voting, and the act states definitely that the employee shall not forfeit his pay for that time. That provision has been in the act for some time, and there has been no protest about it. As a matter of fact, as the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) has said, the employers all over the country have entered into the spirit of the act and have not contested the validity or the legality of that provision. The point I wish to make is this; it is of doubtful validity. In saying that I am not giving my own opinion only, because in the legal sense I do not think it would be considered as worth very much, but those who know something of our laws have
Dominion Elections Act

declared as of doubtful validity an enactment by which the parliament of Canada seeks to bind an employer to pay an employee for something, which is only a matter of contract and therefore falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces. In a matter of at least doubtful validity, when we stretch that period to three hours, the employers of labour might say, "We were willing, without going to the trouble of appearing before the courts, to allow our employees two hours' time, but three hours would be of considerable consequence to us." An employer of labour employing three, four or five thousand hands, might find that the cost would be somewhat excessive. I am under the impression that it is quite likely that some employers might not be willing to comply with the spirit of the act, and might decide to test its validity. In my opinion, and in the opinion of many whom I have consulted, if that is done it will be found to be invalid and the labourer will be in the position where he will not receive any holiday or any pay.

He would not
receive any pay if it were a half holiday?
None at all.
Then he would be no worse off than he would be under the proposed change.

I am not suggesting that
the half holiday would be an ideal arrangement, nor that the previous arrangement of allowing two hours is ideal, but I say that I do not wish to associate myself with the proposed change to three hours for these reasons:	First of all, I do not believe it is
good law, and secondly, I do not believe it is in the interests of the labouring classes. I am not opposed to this principle in any way; if it were possible to grant a half holiday with pay I would be only too willing to do that.
Suppose the act is left as it is, and the day is made a public holiday; could an employer refuse to pay an employee's wages for a period which has been proclaimed to be a public holiday?
Undoubtedly.
I question if he could deduct those wages.

If the contract between
the employer and the employee is a monthly one, then the employee must be paid by the month, no matter how many days are declared to be public holidays; the same principle would apply to a weekly contract.
But not where the employee is being paid by the day?

If he is being paid by the
day, and a half day is declared to be a public holiday, he will only receive pay for the half day that he has worked.

Mr. Chairman, it
may seem to many members to be a matter of small consequence as to whether or not payment shall be made for one hour or two hours, but I think the very fact that we have to debate this matter is an indictment of our present wages system. Many of these men have to pare things down to a very fine * point, and I take it that the real purpose which we have in view is to enable as many as possible of these men to exercise their franchise. Unless provision is made for a certain period when they can take time off, it is impossible for many of them to do so. A great many of the electors in Winnipeg work in the railway shops at Transcona, and in order to vote they must travel a distance of eight or nine miles to Weston, the western suburb of Winnipeg. Unless they have time off it is impossible for them to do that. They should be allowed several hours off, or given a full half holiday. I recognize the fact that there may be some difficulty, as suggested by the chairman of the oommittee, but I can hardly conceive that where the employers are willing to give two hours, they would go to the trouble of appealing against this legislation when one hour only is added to the free time. In case the validity of the act is tested, the worker would be in no worse a position then he would be under the proposed arrangement for a half holiday. It seems to me that we might very well take the chance and give the three hours which would actually meet the requirements Of the time necessary for voting.

The hon. member and myself are in substantial agreement, but it is only a matter of opinion. I give it as my opinion that the employers of labour, when they find they must allow pay for three hours, are not as likely to enter into the spirit of the act, as they have been in the past when they were obliged to allow two hours only. It is my impression that they will test the validity of the act, but that is only my opinion.

Mr. Chairman, the committee in presenting these amendments sought to limit them to proposals on which we were practically unanimous. We sought to avoid bringing before the house at the close of the session any issues which might be disputed.

Dominion Elections Act
Inasmuch as this trouble has arisen, I suggest that the Solicitor General give favourable consideration to the withdrawal of section 4 of this bill repealing section 14 of the original act, and allow the original section 14 to stand.
I think that would, for the present session, be preferable and would allow further consideration of the proposal made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg, when other matters are brought before the house next year, because a number of controversial issues in respect of the Dominion Elections Act must come before us next session in the bill then to be introduced, I understand, by the government.

If there is any
difficulty over validity, is there not a possible difficulty in the Dominion parliament forcing an employer to give a half holiday for election purposes? It seems to me that might readily be construed as interfering with freedom of contract. If objection is taken to the payment of wages for one hour, objection might easily be taken to the cessation of work for half a day.
It is for three hours.

Well, for one or
two or three, I do not care which it is, the principle is the same. If objection is taken to that, objection might be taken to the forced cessation of work and the tieing up of the entire plant for a half day.

This parliament has legislative jurisdiction to declare a holiday or a half holiday for the purpose of carrying out any public business over which parliament has exclusive jurisdiction; that is, such business as a general federal election.

But in practice
that penalizes the worker.

That may be so, but in this case, in order to avoid penalizing the worker any more than he is at present penalized, I would suggest that for the time being we should revert to the terms of the original section 14 of the act, because I think a good deal is to be said in support of the suggestions made by the chairman of the committee which has for some months been considering the bill amending the Dominion Elections Act. That is, if you impose too much upon the employer, you will find that he will contest the matter, whereas at the present time the giving of two hours as a holiday with full pay has become a general standard and accepted. But there is a very strong body of
opposition against extending the time, and as we wish now to reach amendments which are generally acceptable I would suggest that we might drop clause 4 of the bill and allow for the present the original section 14 to stand.

When I suggested this
change to the committee when it was last in session on clause 4 of the bill, I had in mind a situation which became very evident in Winnipeg at the last election. Many of the workers who live in South Winnipeg, St. James, Weston and other western suburbs of the city of Winnipeg, work in the Transcona shops which are from ten to twelve mdes distant from their homes and from the polling subdivisions where they cast their votes. They leave their work at Transcona at three o'clock; it takes them half an hour to an hour to get home; they wash and change, and then they pile into the polling booths in the last hour or so of polling day.

The polls close at six
o'clock.

Yes. The result was that a great number of these men were not able to vote. That was one of the reasons I had in mind for suggesting that the word "two" before the word "hours" in the original section 14 should be struck out and the word "three" substituted therefor. I am not prepared to admit the constitutional invalidity of section 14 of the present act. I think the Dominion parliament, having jurisdiction to legislate with regard to the subject of Dominion elections, may set forth the conditions and circumstances under which the elections shall take place.
There are various contentions both ways, but we cannot decide the matter.

I am not prepared to
admit that section 14 of the present act is ultra vires of this parliament. I think the argument can be made just as strongly for its validity as for its invalidity; in fact, I think the argument for its validity is stronger than that for its invalidity. Rather than see clause 4 of the present bill stand, I would prefer the old section 14 of the present act. If it is the sense of the house, I would prefer, for the reasons I have stated, to have three hours instead of two given to the employees.

Why not extend the
hours of voting?

That might be one
method of meeting the particular difficulty I had in mind, for instance, by extending the
Dominion Elections Act

(polling hours to seven in the evening. I do not know whether the committee has that in *mind or not in any subsequent report that it may bring down.

There is no doubt that the old act gave a special privilege to one particular class. No argument is being advanced to give a farmer two or three hours' pay for going to the polls. No argument is being used to give a fisherman so much extra time to get to the polls. In my judgment, we have stretched our authority in giving the two hours. Let us be content with that. Do not let us exaggerate the thing and ask for so much that we may regret it later. This is a tax upon the employer of labour. If it is proper to give two hours and if it is within the law, as my hon. friend who has just spoken, says, to give three hours, why not half a day, and, if half a day, why not a whole day? Do not make an absurdity of the thing. We have gone far enough. No manufacturer or employer of labour has made a great deal of fuss about the matter. We are giving a good deal; do not let us carry it to an absurdity.

When this clause was
under consideration yesterday, I stated on behalf of the government that, if it were the desire of the house, I saw no objection to the withdrawal of the clause from the bill and to our reverting to the old law. When I made that suggestion, the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) who now moves his amendment, stated that he was not in a position to decide Whether this would be acceptable or not, and the section was allowed to stand, I reiterate that the government has no set opinion; that we are introducing in this case legislation along the lines of the recommendations of the committee. It seems as if this half holiday without pay might not be as satisfactory as the two hours with pay as provided for under the old act.
I am not going to prolong the debate by discussing the question whether we were within our constitutional right in legislating as we did in the past. There is one. side that has been expounded, that is, that salaries and wages are matters of contract and civil rights and, generally speaking, those matters are within the purview of the provinces and not of the Dominion government. But there is also another side that might be urged, and that is that this question of declaring that wages are to be paid during those two hours might be considered as a matter ancillary to the general scheme of legislation regarding elections. These are two viewpoints, one
fMr. Thoreon.]
which would indicate that iwe are not within our jurisdiction, and the other which might indicate that we are perfectly within our province when we have legislated as we have done in the past. I repeat, I am entirely in the hands of the committee and we will stand by the opinion of the committee as it is expressed.

I am in favour of this amendment for various reasons. In the first place I do not think any deduction will be made for the half holiday from the pay of monthly employees such as clerks. With regard to other employees, it is not necessary for any of them to take the half holiday. If a man is employed in the steel works, for instance, and his work is necessary, he can stay at work, and if he works he will get extra time for holidays. I think this should go through as we arranged it in the committee.
With regard to the eight-hour day, I do not see how a man who is working only eight hours a day can take three hours off in the afternoon because that leaves him only one hour to go back and work, and that is hardly worth while. I think the sensible thing to do is to make it a half holiday.
Amendment negatived.

We now have the situation
where we either have to accept the half holiday without pay or the' provision of the existing Dominion Elections Act, and if I have to choose between the two I prefer the existing act to the provisions of the bill now before us.
There is one point that I would like to bring to the attention of the chairman of the special committee. It is rather an important point which he raised. I do not understand much of the law on this question-
Neither does the chairman.

The hon. member (Mr. Power) made the statement here to-day that the validity of the existing act could be challenged and that under the act the worker would not be entitled to two hours with pay. This would raise a very important question. Assume that at some future time some employer or someone interested challenges the act, and that it turns out as the chairman of the committee thought it would turn out. It would mean that hundreds of thousands of electors would have no opportunity on election day of going to the polls and casting their votes. I do not say that anything of that kind will happen, but if it does then it means that we would have to recast completely tho

Dominion Elections Act
provisions of this act. That danger occurred, to my mind, when the chairman of the special committee gave that opinion, either as a lawyer or as the chairman of the committee, I do not know which.

As a very poor lawyer I
gave that opinion.

I do not think, since I have been in this house, that a special committee of the house has ever sat with a more sincere desire to obtain amendments that would be satisfactory to all concerned and that would be fair and impartial to all interests. On this section there were differences of opinion. They arose in this way. All the large corporations employing men and women have a rule almost universal in this oountry that if employees are brought back on a holiday to work they are paid doubfe pay for the time in which they are engaged in such work. Large corporations such as the steel and coal industries cannot shut down for a half day conveniently, and therefore when there is a half holiday they arrange to bring back a certain number of men to keep their works in operation, and they pay them double time. So if we declare this a half holiday a large body of the workingmen and workingwomen of this country who desire to work on that half day will receive employment at double pay for the time in which they are employed.

Is it not possible that it
will have quite the contrary effect to what was intended and that a large number of people will remain at work at double pay rather than go out and vote?

There is the difficulty. We believe in liberty of opinion and liberty of action within certain limits in this country. I am simply stating how this question appeared to the committee. On the other hand, the ordinary day labourer who is employed in the village factory or in the small store in the smaller urban centres has no difficulty whatever in arranging with his employer for ample time to go out and vote. The relations between employers and employees of that class are so amicable in this oountry that very little difficulty has arisen in respect to voting. I prefer the half holiday for this reason, that it assures the hundreds of thousands of men who are employed in the larger factories and the great industries a half holiday for them to go to the poll, and if they are brought back to work for the purpose of carrying on the operations of the company it entitles them to double pay.

A few moments ago the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George was arguing against the amendment of my colleague, and suggesting that it would be wise under the circumstances to leave things as they were, but as soon as the amendment is turned down he suggests that now we adopt the half holiday.

I beg pardon. That is a
mis-representation of my intention. My intention was not to make an argument but to state to the committee the views that influenced us when we were dealing with the matter as a committee.

But the effect is as I stated, whereas a few moments ago the hon. gentleman was suggesting that we leave things as they are; he now suggests an amendment.
I submit that that is hardly a consistent attitude. There may be some truth in what the hon. member has said in regard to a few people in the large industries, but there is a very large number of shops where men are not brought back to work on a holiday. I should say that the vast majority are not brought back and paid double time for the holiday. The suggested plan would work a substantial injustice in their case. It would seem to me that when we remember the very narrow margin on which a great number of the workers have to operate, it is highly desirable that they should be given the opportunity to vote without being penalized too much for so doing. Further than that, I would point out that whilst the relations between employer and employee may in some instances be amicable in many instances they are not of the most cordial nature. It may be all very well to say that a man is free to go and vote, yet in a great many plants a man is not free unless his employer gives him the opportunity. I myself have had difficulty with large employers in that connection who paid no attention to existing legislation for providing suitable hours in which their men could go and vote. They said they could not arrange to let them all go at the same time, and so on. It is quite true I was representing the interests of the employees, but I would take that position whether a man were voting Liberal, Conservative or Labour.

Is the hon. gentleman in
favour of continuing the original section?
Most	decidedly.
We are all agreed.

I think the committee
would be satisfied if we simply dropped the clause, and left the question open; we might attend to it next year. That is section 4, subsection 14.
Dominion Elections Act

I agreed with the clause as
it appears now. I did not take the trouble to look it up myself, but I was informed- I think the information came from the chief electoral officer who appeared before the committee-that this very question was dealt with in the house in 1925, and that by a vote of 54 to 32 the change was then made, and that merely by oversight it was not incorporated in the act. I feel that that being so it would be very proper now to adopt what was done in 1925. I have no very pronounced views on the matter myself, and if they who feel that they have some right to speak for labour think that it would be better to revert to the previous subsection whereby two hours are given with pay I would have no objection to that. On	the	other	hand, I	have nodesire to oppose the suggestion of the Solicitor General that the matter be dropped now, and with many other matters to be attended to which will be subsequently referred to in another report	of	this committee	it mightwell stand to	be	dealt	with at	the next
session of parliament.
Section withdrawn.
On section 20-Name not on the list.

Might I ask the permission
of the committee to refer to another section which oame up yesterday in the house when I was attending a rather important committee? It is a	small	matter but it is
rather important. With the consent of the hon. Solicitor General, who I suppose is in charge of the bill, I would like to insert one word in section 20. If you will refer to section 20 of this bill you will find that it deals with the question of allowing, as it is known in popular parlance, a man or woman to swear himself in on election day. I am talking entirely of rural matters. This does not concern the urban electors at all. There is a privilege there where a man can, as I say, go and swear himself in, on complying with certain formalities, and it is a highly-prized right in those .country places. It is a safeguard against a lot of things; it is a safeguard against corruption, if such should exist, although it does not in the district that I represent; it is a safeguard against carelessness which might exist, or ignorance oif the local deputy returning officer, who has no desire to do an injustice. Under the old act a man went there and he swore, aided by a voter who was on the list, that he had resided in the electoral district the regulation number of days and that he was now a resident in the polling division. Now they have gone further, he has to swear not only that he has been the regulation number of days, and so on,
[Mr. Cannon.3	.
but that so far as he is aware his name does not appear on the list of voters prepared for any other polling division. That is the trouble. Those registrars, as they are called, who put the names of people on the list, are paid so much a head, and sometimes for that reason, and sometimes due to pure carelessness, they just take the last list, or some other list, and they jam on every name that is there, men who have been away for years, or men who have been dead for years. They do not put them on deliberately; they simply take the list and will not be bothered checking up to see whether Bill Jones has left the district, or has gone to heaven or to some other place in the meantime. Then the man comes along on election day and wants to vote in this other polling division where he has been residing for perhaps six months. He knows his name is on the old list, or someone tells him so; he may be aware that he is left on the old list, but-improperly. What is he going to do? He has no remedy; he loses his vote. That is not the intention of this amendment.
He can vote at the polling division where he belongs.

But he does not want to.
He cannot afford to take a long trip. His interests are in the polling division where he then resides. We are proposing to make it easy for the workingman, and for everyone, to vote. I would ask the Solicitor General to be permitted to insert this one word. It is not the way I would like to have it, but I know it would open up a lot of discussion to change the whole section. I would ask leave to insert the word "properly" down on the second last line of the section, so that it will read that the man has got to swear that so far as he is aware, his name does not "properly" appear on any other list. There is no opportunity for abuse; he has to have someone who lives there swear to his identity. He has got to swear himself that he has resided in that polling division. It is rather a retrogade step from the old act. If the Solicitor General would allow me to put in that one word "properly" it would, in great part, meet my objection.

I have no objection. I
think that would improve the section.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.

May I. ask the
chairman of the committee whether the committee gave any consideration to the question of proportional representation which question,
I think, was presented to the committee.
We had a speech on it yesterday before this committee.

The committee did give
some consideration to the question of proportional representation. We even invited representatives of labour to appear before us to give us their views on it. They did speak briefly. We also heard another witness who told us what he thought of proportional representation, but the committee did not see fit to change our present system.

Nor to introduce so controversial a question where we were anxious for unanimity.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Vote No. 93-Railways, to provide for additional car ferry and facilities for car ferry service between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, $3,500,000. This vote, on motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) last evening has been reduced by $1,000,000. Shall the item carry?
I think this includes the estimate for a new ferry.
Yes.

Some reference was made to this matter last evening, and since then I have refreshed my memory with regard to the accounting in connection with the ferry service between the mainland and Prince Edward Island. I wish to quote from page 28 of the report of the royal commission on maritime claims. The particular reference to which I wish to direct the attention of the minister is this:
We further recommend that, so far as the ferry boat service is concerned, it should not be run as part of the railway operations, but should be run by the railway administration under separate account for the department. We feel that, by reason of its association with railway accounts, this service does not get the attention it should receive.
This bears out substantially what was represented to the minister last night. Now at the present time the operative charges are included in the accounts of the railway lines on the eastern division, and it is recommended otherwise in the Duncan report. Not only that; it is fair and reasonable that the operative charges should not be included in the eastern lines operating account, where it
Supply-Railways-Car Ferry
does not properly belong. The reason is obvious: it makes a much larger deficit in these accounts than otherwise would be fairly represented. I do not think the minister has any particular objection except the difficulty of accounting. I believe his attitude is one of preparedness to recognize that, provided the difficulties of accounting are not too great. He says there are very considerable difficulties in the matter of separate accounting.
There is, of course, no difficulty in separate accounting for expenditures. The only difficulty relates to separate accounting so far as revenues are concerned.
I take it there are difficulties at any rate.
Entirely in relation to revenue.
The recommendation of the Duncan report is that the accounting be separate. The minister says that will not be an easy matter. There is nothing more unsatisfactory than the present method.
Why?

Because it heaps up the deficits in the operative expenses on the eastern division of the railways and makes the apparent deficit larger than it actually is. Another reason is contained in the Duncan report; that is, that more attention would be given this important service. I submit that some other method than the present should be adopted; it is absolutely the worst so far as having the true results of operative expenses on the eastern lines is concerned. The minister says there are difficulties, whatever they may be, in the accounting. It seems to me that accountants possess considerable powers of adaptability and resourcefulness, and surely they can arrive at some system whereby the accounts will be kept separate without too much expense and too much labour. If there are difficulties-and on that score I cannot express an opinion-I believe they should be overcome, or at least an attempt should be made to overcome them. I would even go the length of suggesting, if this is the last recourse, that the operative expenses on the car ferry service be arrived at in a fair way by estimate, allowing that amount to be written off the operative expenses of the eastern lines.

I am not prepared bo admit for a moment that the deficit on the eastern lines is largely inflated by the operating loss on the ferry.
Supply-Railways-Car Ferry
It is to that extent.

No one knows to what extent it exists. I think we can get the exact cost of operating the ferry; I believe it is in the neighbourhood of $200,000 a year. That is the oost of operating the ferry, exclusive of interest and depreciation, which, of course, is taken care of by the fact that the ferry is built out of an appropriation by this parliament. No interest is charged to the railway with respect to the cost of this ferry or the cost of the work; it is borne by parliament. Therefore, so far as interest on capital is concerned, that interest does not operate to increase the deficit on the eastern lines; so that the operating cost is the only matter to consider.
That is the only point I have raised.

The last legal process to
which the minister refers would hardly be fair. This, if I recall aright, was a homestead taken up by a man called Beach about twenty or twenty-five years ago. In those days, to go there was quite a trip for anyone to take. He went there; I think he took his wife with him and they lived on the property for some years. While there necessarily was not very much clearing or farming of the property, because there is not much of that done at Fort Churchill, nevertheless the man lived there and settled on the property, having in mind, as far as I can judge, the fact that some day Fort Churchill was destined to be the site of a city or a town, a point of export. That foresight on his part, his efforts to get there and the time he spent there are worth something. He was, in other words, a typical pioneer. The railway comes along and decides that Fort Churchill is to be the railway

I think his father died later, but Beach held this property. The minister shakes his head. There is no doubt that the property was held under the control of Beach in some form. That is not acquiring property for railway purposes. Mark you, I am not complaining because the government took control of the townsite, because I think the minister's objective was to prevent unwise speculation in townsite property in a prospective terminal. Instead of simply taking the property over as an abandoned homestead, it should have been regarded as part of what would be a valuable townsite, because if the government is going to exercise control over that town-site and reap the full benefit which some people think in future years will be very great, these property owners are certainly entitled to a very different basis of valuation than simply as land taken over for railway purposes. The point I am making is this: This man's lands were taken from him compulsorily, without his consent. Secondly, the crown, as distinguished from the railway company, filed expropriation proceedings against the whole of that land regardless of whether it was required for railway purposes or not. I think it is proper to use that word "regardless," because it is not asserted by the railway that these lands were to be used for railway purposes. Had it been a private enterprise taking over these lands without the consent of the owner, then under section 171 of the Railway Act, which was inserted in the Act at the instance of Judge Mafoee, then chairman of the railway commission, the notice would have lapsed and they would have had

to start de novo to take the lands, and the principle with regard to compensation would govern as from the date of the filing of the new notice, which, of course, changes the whole situation, as the minister will see. It is because of the long delay in taking the proceedings, which the minister now says was partly attributable to the owners themselves, that I was endeavouring to bring the matter to his attention. I am frank to say that I know very little about it except what was told to me by a gentleman whom I have often met travelling up and down this country for the last twenty-five years. What the minister says about the lots having been sold is true, but multiply the number of cases by five or six hundred and you get into an intolerable situation. The crown when it expropriates, as distinguished from a railway company that expropriates, has been offering compensation that poor unfortunate people have been compelled to take, and which they would not take at all from a railway company where they could take proceedings before the local district court judge and have compensation fixed in the local court. But people who are not in good circumstances naturallly think with much doubt and diffidence of approaching the exchequer court, because they cannot afford to go into litigation against the crown. They have not the facilities. I direct attention to that, because I do not think those people have been treated with the consideration that would be accorded to them were they the owners of property that had been taken from them without their consent by a private railway company.

What would my hon.
friend suggest I might now do?

I think what might be
done is to revise the whole basis upon which compensation has been offered. This is not in the hon. minister's department, but in the Department of National Defence; a situation arose in North Vancouver, and I must say I feel very sorry for the poor Old lady who had a lot out there for which she paid several hundred dollars. They appropriated and she lost her property. She said, give me another lot equal to this but, of course, that was not done. I think she got less than $100. This is a case in which the basis of compensation is wholly inadequate.

I have seen a good many expropriation proceedings. I am not speaking of this case at all, but one or two things in
connection with expropriation proceedings have struck me rather forcibly for a number of years. I notice in practically all expropriation proceedings, and probably there is a good defence for the attitude, that the judges, whoever they may be, whether exchequer or county court judges before whom expropriation proceedings of any kind are taken, invariably hear a good deal of evidence as to the utility value at that moment. Frequently it can be shown before these courts that the actual utility value is very, very little, and as a consequence some man who had the foresight perhaps fifteen or twenty years before to purchase a piece of property with the prophetic idea that it was going to be required by a railway or some other company, has that property taken from him for practically nothing, although not only the original purchase but the carrying charges may have cost him a good deal of money. I have seen not one but many cases where properties were expropriated, and that was the ultimate result to the man concerned. I admit that in many instances a railway or a government may require property for very good and sufficient reasons, and in that case it is right to expropriate. But this is the principle I wish to offer as my suggestion-not in regard to this case but in regard to cases in general: I do not believe that either the government or the railways in this country should expropriate property at any time unless there is absolute need for that property. That, in my opinion, is a principle that should be laid down. I have seen cases of expropriation where the railway, or the person concerned for whom the expropriation took place, did not have actual need of the property in question, and this would appear to be such a case. A large area of land was taken for the purpose of preventing speculation; I remember reading something of it in the press, and I think I am right in that. There probably is a good defence of such a course, but there is also a good defence of speculation. If some man had the foresight to see that some day the land would be valuable, I rather think it a good argument that his foresight should be taken into consideration, a thing which is very rarely done before any of the courts I have seen adjudicating on expropriations.

Since the minister has
raised the question as to the principle of expropriating property to save people from themselves, I want to voice my objection. He says the minister autocratically -he uses the language of Lord Dunedin, or some other lord, but I would like to read the whole of the judgment before I would accept that part of it as being the complete expression of Lord Dunedin's opinion; that would only be fair. And then my hon. friend says there is a law, " thou shalt not steal," with the plain inference that the government was stealing this property from those people. That was the clear insinuation of my hon. friend. After all, what is the fact? The government says it was in the best interests of
this country, having regard to all the peculiar circumstances surrounding Fort Churchill, for the state to take this land. And there is a statute which my hon. friend read, the Expropriation Act, which enables a minister of the crown	to file expropriation plans. Those plans were filed. Then my hon. friend stops and says dramatically, " thou shalt not steal." He knows perfectly well that no stealing is either intended or possible. The Exchequer Court Act was passed by this parliament. Why? To insure that in cases where the government of the day decided in its wisdom, or lack of it, that a certain piece of property was required for governmental purposes, machinery should be available by which the rights of the subject could be protected. My hon. friend says,
" thou shall not steal." Does he attach any importance whatever to the fact that there is an exchequer court in Canada, one of the high courts of this country, set up specifically for the purpose of insuring that nothing shall be unjustly taken from the subject by the crown? The minister did not take this property, the government did not take it, without compensation. The government took it subject to the provisions of the Expropriation Act and subject to the decision of the Exchequer Court of Canada as to the value of the property, which, when determined, will \ be paid to the owners thereof.
In fact most of the discussion this afternoon on this matter, Mr. Chairman, is out of order, because the subject matter of the value of this property is now under adjudication by one of the high courts of this Dominion. Nothing that we say here should affect, at any rate, the judgment to be rendered by that court.. I know that the exchequer court will not, as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition intimated, steal this property or allow the crown to steal it from the people who own it. If it were possible for the government to steal the property of any individual I should be one of the first to cooperate with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in setting up machinery to prevent it. Neither the crown nor anyone else has the right to steal. But " stealing " is an entirely wrong word to use in connection with a transaction of this kind.
I do not know that we can, with advantage, further discuss the matter. It is before the court. There is one way in which it could be dealt with here, and that is by a motion, on the part of members who feel as strongly as the leader of the opposition does that this policy is a wrong policy, that the proceedings for the expropriation of the privately-owned property on the peninsula at Fort Churchill

I wish to make some remarks with regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr Thorson). I had not intended to speak, but the remarks made by the minister in reply to the hon. memlber for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) raised a doubt in my mind as to the appraisal of the situation by the minister. I should like to impress upon him that the public of Manitoba are very much exercised hbout this matter, and I should not like the minister or the house to think that this is a question of connecting Churchill with Winnipeg. It is a broader question than that; it affects the connecting of southern Manitoba with northern Manitoba. Unfortunately nature has
divided Manitoba in a diagonal fashion by the great lakes of Manitoba, an obstruction which has not been felt in years gone by. for the reason, as everyone knows, that northern Manitoba was but a hazy possibility until two or three years ago. But with development in mining north of The Pas, and with the prospective seaport at Churchill, northern Manitoba has become the land of hope and glory for southern Manitoba, and we are all very much disturbed in our minds as to the immediate future.
Manitoba, as all hon. members know, is very restricted in an agricultural sense. We have pretty well reached the extent of development agriculturally, and the opening up of the northern part of the province in the last few years has created a new spirit throughout Manitoba. But we find that there is just a possibility of this prospect vanishing from before our eyes, because we have no railway connection whatsoever between north and south. The great lakes, as I say, cut our province practically in two.
I do not think there is any public question so vital to Manitobans at the present time as this one. The hon. member for Dauphin will agree with me that there is no subject on which it is easier to call together a public meeting than this one; irrespective of party, we are all deeply concerned and interested. I should not like, therefore, to have the impression go abroad, from what the minister said in reply to the hon. member for Dauphin, that he is not thoroughly apprised of the state of public opinion in that province. I do not think he meant it in that way, but it seems to me that he conceived there was no haste, that there was considerable time in which to discuss the matter, and that no decisive step was necessary this year. If that is so, the minister ought to revise his attitude. I believe that public opinion is so unanimous in Manitoba and so much in earnest that the minister ought to pay very close attention to this matter and do something substantial this year. An investigation ought to be set on foot. I think the investigation could be easily finished this year so that the question of some concrete scheme might be faced next year, and I do not think the problem is so very big.
I am sorry these alternative schemes mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre have entered into the question and created some difficulty. I do not think the combined water and rail route should be considered at all; I think it is one of those fanciful propositions which really might be swept aside at once. As for the

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
Gypsumville proposition, that has considerable merit, but the minister will admit that it means the construction of an entirely new Hudson Bay railway, a proposition which I think parliament will not be likely to consider for some years. However, I would remind the minister that the original Hudson Bay railway, which runs through the length and breadth of old Manitoba, is still in existence and that with very little adaptation, very little straightening out and the addition of cut-offs it could be made a very effective connection between northern and southern Manitoba. It would have advantages to which the other routes cannot lay claim at all. The old Canadian Northern runs diagonally across Manitoba to the west of the lakes and connects up the most fertile, productive and picturesque parts of that province. In addition to that, there is almost a direct connection between Winnipeg and The Pas which, as far as I can see, for all future time will be the basis for the great mining development in that country.
_ I would not like the minister to think this is simply a matter of connecting Port Churchill and Winnipeg; in its broader aspect it is a question of provincial patriotism. We feel that we do not want to be deprived of the advantages which for all these years we have imagined would be ours. It would be strange irony if the province which has been foremost in advocating the Hudson Bay railway should be finally deprived of those advantages, which certainly will be the case if within the next few years some way is not found to connect us up more directly with the Hudson Bay Railway and with the other developments in that northern country. I am afraid all the forecasts made during my advocacy of the Hudson Bay railway in this house in years gone by will fall short of fulfilment if we do not very shortly get some connection with the road.
As I have already said, I do not want to leave with the minister the impression that I think he is treating this matter too lightly, but his rather offhand reply to the hon. member for Dauphin made me feel that his attitude would create a great deal of dissatisfaction back home in Manitoba.

I am sorry if the brevity of my replies to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Dauphin gave the impression of offhandedness. I can assure my hon. friend that continuous representations in connection with these matters have been made to me during the last several months, especially by the hon. members from Manitoba, and I had no intention of conveying the idea that I did not 
regard the whole matter as one of very serious importance. I certainly do so regard it. If it were as simple from the point of view of the people of Manitoba generally as it is to my hon. friend from Nelson, who would build a connection from Mafeking to The Pas as the most satisfactory solution, the proposition would not be so difficult, but unfortunately the people of Manitoba do not agree that that is a satisfactory solution of the difficulty. I am not prepared to say, and no one else is prepared to say, what is the best thing to do having regard to the situation which has developed; I will go further and say that none of us will be able correctly to estimate what is best until we know more about the volume of inbound traffic via the bay and the ocean rates which will prevail. By that I do not mean that there should be any delay in tackling this problem, but I do say that this one uncertain factor is of very considerable importance in connection with its solution.
If I had desired to be so offhand as my hon. friend feared I was, I might easily have said that this was a proper problem for the management of the Canadian National Railways. I did not do so because of a recognition on my part and on the part of the government that the Hudson bay policy is a matter of government policy rather than of Canadian National Railway policy, although it must be remembered that all the connections at every point south of The Pas are Canadian National connections, and I am not sure that as a parliament we can undertake the building of another Hudson Bay railway down into the southern area, as my hon. friend indicated.
I think he said that he doubted whether it would be possible to bring the government portion of the Hudson Bay road, as distinct from the Canadian National portion, south to Winnipeg. I am inclined to agree that before embarking on any project of that kind the government would have to consider very seriously many different aspects of the question. I did not tell my hon. friend from Dauphin to go to the Canadian National management, as I would have done in connection with an ordinary branch line, for the reason I have indicated, because at present this is a matter of government policy. Because of that fact I am prepared from a departmental point of view to investigate all these possible solutions and I will give the assurance that this investigation will be undertaken just as soon as we can organize for it. It was only when my hon. friend from Dauphin tried, with very good grace, to pin me down to a definite time for completing

that investigation that I refused to be bound, and I think the house will appreciate that it is very difficult for me to be definite in that regard, bearing in mind the volume of work on hand in the department in connection with the Hudson Bay railway and many other great undertakings in various parts of the country.

In connection with the

My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre obtained information in the special committee on railways and shipping with regard to the contracts let by the Canadian National in that regard. With respect to the port itself no contracts have been let; the work is being done and has been done by the forces of the department up to the present.

That is, the work on the

Does the minister formally
approve the contracts negotiated by the Canadian National Railways before they become effective ?

If my hon. friend will ask the question I will answer it, even though it means that it is being answered for a second time.
If it has been answered already in this house then the minister is justified in his attitude.

I thought my hon.
friend would be satisfied to know where it could be found.

I thought the hon. minister
was complaining that I am going over ground which has been already covered before a small committee of eight members; if that is going to be his attitude, then I shall certainly be an objector to any such committee.

If he desires me to repeat that information I shall be happy to do so, but it is already printed in the evidence. If my hon. friend will repeat his question I will be glad to answer it.

answers can be found, that might hasten matters. I would like to know what portion of last year's vote was spent in contracts and what portion was spent on day labour.

In order to answer that question intelligently it will be necessary to separate the two pieces of work, the railway and the port. In connection with the railway, the grading work was the subject of tender. Seven tenders were received and the lowest tenderer received the contract for the work at the price of $1,270,100. With respect to all the other work .on the railway it was done entirely by Canadian National forces on a day labour basis in the same way as the Canadian National carry out similar work for themselves. The department audits the day labour costs of the Canadian National on the work and the department pays the amount necessary to meet the accounts of the Canadian National in that regard.

Is it not a new departure for a railway company to construct its line by day labour? Has it not always been recognized as being the best practice to call for tenders for certain sections of the line and let the contracts to the lowest responsible bidders?

That fs true with respect to grading, and that is being done by the Canadian National at the present time in connection with all their work. The balance of the work such as ballasting, track laying, small bridges, culverts and telegraph lines is all done by Canadian National forces on a day labour basis. I am not sure of the practice of other roads, but I believe it is the same. For instance, large steel bridges would be matters of contract as my hon. friend can well understand that the day labour force of the railway would not be equipped to do work such as that. The practice followed here is the practice which has been followed by the Canadian National for some years in connection with their work, and it has-been found to be satisfactory in operation.

I assume that engineers' estimates are given for particular sections of the line before the work is commenced. Will the minister state whether or not those estimates have been exceeded, and if so, in what instances and by how much?

In answering my hon.
friend's question, we have to take into account the character of a large portion of this work. Some 332 -miles of the railway were, as my hon. friend knows, built a considerable number of years ago and were allowed to fall into

very bad disrepair. That matter was alt threshed out in the house during each of the last two sessions, and to estimate accurately what would be required to rehabilitate the old track, a large portion of which was not and could not be used for many years, was a matter of some difficulty. I do not think I have available the original estimate of the cost of rehabilitation which is, of course, the major factor. I can give the estimate of the cost of completion of the line from the Limestone river to Churchill, because that is all new work. Up to date I believe I am correct in stating that it is reasonably close to the estimate. Of course the work is in process of being carried out and it is impossible to give final figures in connection with that part of the work which is new work, that is the only new work on the railway.

Will the minister give the
committee, then, the original estimate for the rehabilitation of the line and the actual cost?
The rehabilitation is not yet completed, but I will give such information as I can.
Has the minister any information to indicate whether or not the estimates of the engineers are being exceeded?

The original estimate is
likely to be exceeded with respect to the rehabilitation of the old line to mile 332. That statement is subject to the qualification that it dtepends upon what may happen with respect to subsequent settlement of embankments where the later are founded on frozen material which may disintegrate over a period of years. Then we have on the new portion of the line a problem which is also a qualification, namely, the possible cost of dealing with snow trouble a-cross thirty-odd miles of open tundra. That is, there are thirty-odd miles of completely open country which, in those latitudes, produces a special snow problem that may add somewhat to the cost. There is a third qualification applying to the old line, namely, a possible cost of putting gravel ballast between mile 100 and mile 356, rather than leaving the present sand ballast, because in that area there is a stretch of the line which does not happen to contain locally adjacent ballast pits, and so far the best locally available material, pretty sandy in character, has been used. If the order is given to use gravel ballast drawn from considerable distances, that will be a qualification tending to increase the expenditure.
