Has the minister an approximate estimate of the amount by which the original estimate of the engineers will be exceeded? There must be some report on that.

As nearly as I can gather from the reports of the Canadian National engineers with respect to the matter, the original estimated cost to build the line from mile 356 to Churchill, that is what I call the new railway, was $7,543,000. It is not expected that that item will be exceeded save as affected by the qualification which I mentioned a few moments ago. With respect to the rehabilitation, the figures I have are of an inclusive character, including both the old line and the new, and I am trying to separate them as I go along, although it is somewhat difficult to do so. The present estimate of $29,300,000 to rehabilitate and also to complete the line to Churchill includes original cost figures, the cost of building the line originally. There is an estimated expenditure, from April 1, 1926, of $13,973,000, indicating an additional cost of $2,700,000 against the estimate for the lower standard, or about $1,362,000 greater than the estimated cost for the higher standard.

I must confess that I am completely in the dark. I asked the minister whether he 'had an estimate of how much it would cost to rehabilitate the line. Let us fix that matter now. That was not my whole question. I asked him how much the original estimate for the rehabilitation of the line would be exceeded. I suggested to him that he must have from the engineers some statement as to the approximate amount by which the original estimate would be exceeded. I am now suggesting that we start at the beginning. Will the minister state what was the engineers' original estimate of cost for the rehabilitation of the line?

There were a number of qualifications, as my hon. friend will remember, to engineers' estimating upon such an, uncertain proposition as rehabilitation. I am now having the black records searched to see whether we have any definite estimates from any engineers at any time as to what it would cost to rehabilitate the old line. My hon. friend will understand there were no standards whatever to apply to such a job. In some cases the cost was greater than it would have been to build an entirely new line. Then there would be stretches that would not be so bad. The best information I can give to my hon. friend is in this form.
This is an old estimate by the Canadian National as to what might be required:
IA.	Branch line standard rehabilitation from LePas to mile 332, $3,000,000.
IB.	Better standard and facilities for heavier traffic Le Pas to mile 332, $4,373,000.
The total estimated cost, inclusive of the line to Churchill-that is the awkiward feature because new line and rehabilitated line are used everywhere in the figures I have before me-is $12,611,000.
We are not in a position to say that that cost is being exceeded, until we get further along with the work but from the reports of cost we anticipate that difficulties of the kind that I referred to a little while ago, will develop to a point which may involve higher cost on the rehabilitated portion of the line than the estimate.
It appeans, however, at the present time that the new line from mile 356 to Churchill may be expected to be completed reasonably within the figure I gave of $7,543,000. As I pointed out, our experience in those northern latitudes is that it is not possible to say with certainty when you finish a line, that it is really finished; that is, troubles are likely to develop in subsequent years and to require to be adjusted by capital expenditures.
Apparently the major portion of this work consists of rehabilitating the line. The minister is unaJhle to tell the committee what was the original estimate for the rehabilitation of that line?
That is the figure I gave.
I want to be sure about this. I understood the minister to say that the cost of rehabilitation and of building a new line to Churchill was $12,600,000.
That is rehabilitation and constructing a new line.
Exactly.
Of which $4,373,000 was the original estimate for rehabilitation.

No; that $3,000,000 was for another standard, a lower standard. If one standard were adopted, the cost would be $3,000,000. If another standard were adopted, the cost would be $4,373,000. The question is not one of adding the two amounts together.
Then the estimated cost of rehabilitation is $4,373,000 on one 'basis and $3,000,000 on another. Which basis was adopted?

The higher.

I can best answer that
by taking an estimate here given that it may exceed the amount originally estimated by about $1,362,000.
That would be about 30 per cent more than the original estimate. I am correct in that, am I not?

The original estimate was
$4,373,000, and it is estimated that that will he exceeded by $1,362,000, which is roughly 30 per cent in excess of the original estimate. Apparently all this work on the Hudson Bay railway is being done on this basis-estimate, day labour, and then later we face excessive cost. Certainly we do in this case up to about 30 per oent. A contractor is bound to give a more accurate estimate than that. We could ask numerous contractors for their estimates, and the one who gives the lowest estimate could be tied down to that amount, and he would not be paid an excessive cost to the amount of $1,362,000 as in this case. I think my hon. friend
wants to be fair, but again he is confusing two things-the reconstruction or rehabilitation of the old line and the building of that portion of the line which is new. He is basing his criticism upon an engineer's estimate which was made on the cost of rehabilitation. I am critical of engineers as a general rule, but I certainly think they cannot be criticized very severely in connection with an attempt to estimate what it will cost to rehabilitate 350 miles of railway over muskeg, with all the variable conditions of the track. That was an effort to give us something to guide us, and the engineers made it quite clear that there were none of the usual factors present which would enable them to estimate with any degree of accuracy. When it came to building neiw track we did let a contract, but my hon. friend is surely not under th|e impression that any contractor would make a bid for building a road through that country on a lump sum basis and stand by it. The Canadian National is doing the work under virtually the same conditions as those upon which a contractor would undertake it; that is, a unit price, so much per yard for this, that and the other material. A contractor would never think of tying himself down to a lump price for the whole job.
I realize that.

When my hon. friend
draws the conclusion that we could have saved money by letting a contract for this rehabilitation to some firm other than the Canadian National, I cannot agree with him at all. If we had asked for tenders for that work, in view of all the variable factors connected with it and the different kinds of work involved, we would have had to pay mure than it will cost us to have it done by the Canadian National, with experienced forces and equipment of their own. If we had let a contract for that rehabilitation to some outside contractor we would have had to pay interest on the equipment and all that sort of thing. The Canadian National has the equipment in its own service and hence could perform and did perform that service more economically than a contractor could possibly have done.
The minister, then, is of the opinion that day labour is more economical than tender and contract?

My hon. friend knows that I did not say that. In connection with this piece of work, being of the character it is, it was more economical for us to get the

Canadian National's regular forces to do that work for us, paying them actually what it cost them, than it would have been to let a contract to a contractor who 'because of the uncertainty of the volume and character of the work involved would undoubtedly have allowed a tremendous margin for safety in addition to his ordinary profit.
A lot of the new work is being let on the day labour basis, is it not?
No.
I understood the minister to say that only the grading had been let by contract.
That is right.
And that the remainder, the terminals and the laying of steel, was being done by day labour. Am I correct in that?

So far as the terminals, the roundhouses and that sort of thing are concerned, the Canadian National follows the same practice as it does with simiLar structures on its own lines. That class of work is done by contract. But again, I repeat, there are certain kinds of work which the Canadian National management, who are experts in this work, and who have proven by their successful management of the road that they know what they are about, have found can be most economically done by day labour; and we take their word for it that the application of precisely the same principles by the same men is the best and most economical way of building this new road.
Are the terminals being built by day labour?
When my hon. friend says terminals, just what does he mean?

I understand that this estimate . that, we are considering is for the Hudson Bay railway and terminals. I think the minister should be in a much better position than I to say what the terminals are. He has the information surely; I have not, and I am asking him. If there are no terminals, why is the word "terminals" used in this vote? It is a substantial amount, $6,500,000. What are we voting this money for if there are no terminals? If there are terminals what are they and how are they being built?
Mr. DUNNING': Surely my hon. friend is not serious, but I will try to comply with hi3 request for information in so far as I can, and in so far as his questions are reasonable.
Does the minister say it is unreasonable for me to ask what the terminals consist of, when the word "terminals" is used in this vote?

I understand fully my hon. friend's object, and I will try to be as courteous as I can in helping him to attain it. My hon. friend started by asking whether the terminals were being built by day labour. I asked him what he had in his mind when he asked the question regarding terminals.
The terminals that are being built under this vote.

I will try again. Such
structures as the Canadian National, for their own railway, would have built by contract- I have in mind roundhouses or station buildings-are being let to contract by the Canadian National in the case of the Hudson Bay railway. Such work as would be done on the Canadian National lines by the company's own forces is being done by the company's own forces in this case. All the work which is at present- being carried on by the departmental forces in connection with the harbour terminals, the dredging work, and so forth, is being done by day labour.

I wonder if the minister
could tell whether in the committee the list of the contracts which have been let and are outstanding was given, with amounts.

No, it was not asked
for. I can supply that readily..
I should like to have that.

I do not know that I
have it before me. There-was just the grading contract, and I believe there was one contract for a steel bridge-

The minister stated that
the contract had been let for roundhouses, for instance. He now states that only the grading contract-

I was going on, if my
hon. friend ih-ad not interrupted me, to speak -of the possibility of there being contracts in connection with roundhouses. I know my hon. friend does not want to delay me, and that he is serious in seeking all this information, and I am very anxious indeed to give it to him. We have not at the moment a list of all the contracts let by the Canadian National Railways up to the present time. Such a list will be secured and will be supplied later, if possible to-day.

This money is being voted by .parliament, and it is being voted for a



Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
government undertaking. The Auditor General, therefore, should have control over the expenditure so far as this work is concerned. Is there any evidence, other than the payment to the Canadian National Railways, by which we can check it up in the public accounts?

My hon. friend is quite
right in stating that this being an expenditure by the government of Canada, of the funds of Canada, it is subject to the audit of the Auditor General. As to the agency relationship, the department, I presume under the direction of the Auditor General,-which is the same arrangement as exists in the department itself,-that is, under our own auditing staff, audits the accounts of the Canadian National Railways as presented to us, the day labour sheets, and all that sort of thing, in the same manner as the departmental audit staff deals with any other expenditure that is in progress.

That partly answers the
question I am asking. To-day we vote, we will say, three millions dollars for the Hudson Bay railways. To what extent has this parliament, through the public accounts committee, the power next year to examine those accounts? As I see it, none at all.

Offhand, I do not know
what the legal position is, but I would certainly expect the public accounts to have authority to examine everything. That would be my attitude absolutely.
Is it not a fact that the moneys are paid to the Canadian National Railways ?
Yes.

And that all we have
control over is that the Canadian National Railways get the money, and we have no way of checking its expenditure of that money.
I consent to the principle right now that we are entitled to follow their expenditures right to the end when they are acting as agents for the crown in this matter.

The minister sees the
the difficulty, does he not? If we had the expenditure made by the government direct to a contractor-and the Canadian National Railways must occupy that position either as contractor or as agent-wc would then have in the public accounts committee all the IMr. Bennett.]
expenditures made in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. At the moment all we have is a check to the Canadian National Railways; the Auditor General's report does not deal with that money so far as I can ascertain.

I am advised that the
amounts paid to the Canadian National Railways are itemized in the public accounts.

Part of them; and in
that connection I could not quite follow the answer given 'by the minister to my hon. friend from Vancouiver-Burrard (Mr. Clark)

That is what I am
advised. Quite frankly I have not checked up on that feature of it, but I have no doubt at all as to the .matter, particularly with respect to the public accounts committee having the right to follow these expenditures completely to the end. And1 I am advised that details of the amounts paid to the Canadian National Railways are given in. the public accounts.

That is right, but the
answer to a question asked by my hon. friend from Vancouver-Burrard is certainly at variance with that understanding.

I do not recollect the
answer.

There is a dredge at
Port Nelson at the end of a pier. I think it cost one million dollars delivered at Nelson, did it not?

I will get the accurate
information. There are many years ot history behind this project, and it is very difficult to have everything here.

I do not want to press
the minister to answer what he is not in a position to answer. My advice is that the dredge cost something like one million dollars and is lying across the pier, thirty feet at each end, with just enough extension at one end to balance the machinery at the other, and the dredge is in good shape. But another dredge was purchased and 'brought in to be used at Churchill, and two new lighters from eastern Canada were brought to Churchill although there were boats at Nelson which, while a little out of repair, could easily have been put in commission. That is a matter about which I should like a statement from the minister.

I do not know the
original cost of the suction dredge. My best advice is that it was delivered to the govern-

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
ment of that day at some point in eastern Canada at a cost of $270,000, to which must be added, of course, the cost of taking it up there, which would be very considerable. I do not want again to appear condemnatory of previous governments in regard to what was done, but my answer to my bon. friend may involve some iitble criticism in that connection. However, I will relate the facts as I know them. The material to be dredged at either Churchill or Nelson cannot be successfully and economically handled by a suction dredge. That was proven in the effort to use the suction dredge in question at Nelson, and the material at Churchill does not differ very much from the material at Nelson. I have related in this house before the circumstances of the storm which occurred before my time, and resulted in the dredge landing in its present position, substantially as stated by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.. As to the suggestion of my hon. friend that it could easily be taken down and at little expense, I should like to say that the engineers are not agreed as to how that dredge is to be taken down from its present position either economically or safely. In view of the fact that it was certainly not suitable for any work we had up there, I did not deem it the part of wisdom to spend money on it at the present time, and, instead, secured the kind of dredge which everyone agrees can handle the type of work requiring to be done at Churchill.
Were they purchased?
The contract let for the building, yes.

Who supplied the new
dredges?
The Canadian Vickers.

There were two, I am
informed.
Yes.
What did they.cost?

Churchill No. 1, $357,500; Churchill No. 2, $360,650. My hon. friend read or made some statement with regard to lighters at Nelson which might have been used and were not. I want to assure him that all floating plant there which was at all serviceable was put into shape and moved to Churchill and is there a-t the present time. There is left at Nelson no floating plant which is usable.

We have a dump scow that is new, and a barge, and we got another scow from the Department of Public Works. The rest of the equipment, outside of tugs, is the equipment which was at Nelson and which is being put into shape. We had also at Nelson one tug which has been reconditioned and is in use at Churchill.
Was there a fire in the roundhouse at Churchill last summer?

No; my hon. friend's
informant is evidently referring to what I mentioned in the house last winter. I gave then an account of a fire which had occurred in the roundhouse at Nelson, not at Churchill.
Then there has been no fire at Churchill since the 'operations were commenced there, by which any locomotives or materials were destroyed?
The fire occurred at Nelson.
It is advisable to clear this point up, not for my purposes but for the information of those who may read it and wish to be satisfied as to what the facts are.
The fire was at Neison.
Would the government be in any sense responsible for the care of labourers who went to Churchill in the summer of 1928?
What does my hon. friend mean by "care"?

There were eighty-five workmen who were supposed to be at Churchill last year, including store bosses, blacksmith bosses, tractor bosses and superintendents and foremen. My information, given me by a reputable citizen desiring to find out the facts, is that twenty out of the eighty-five were superintendents and foremen, while the rest were labourers. The foremen received eighty cents an hour and worked fourteen hours a day and the labourers received forty cents in the warmer weather and forty-five in the colder and paid a dollar a day for board. We will leave it at that for the moment. Would the department know anything about this, or would it be the Canadian National Railways?
If what my hon. friend is stating relates to Churchill-
Yes, Churchill.

-then the workmen at the port would be departmental.

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
That is what I am advised.

If they were working on the railway they would be Canadian National people. If my hon. friend would give me a copy of his statement I should be glad to have the facts ascertained and submitted to him.

The statement sent to me is interlarded with observations and queries, and I could not detach the statement itself. I am anxious to ascertain whether or not the Department of Railways and Canals carried on operations at Churchill in the summer of 1928, what wages were paid, and whether there was a doctor in charge of the men.
Yes.

How many men were
there? Then there is another question-
Will my hon. friend ask the questions one by one? I have a record of all the operations at Churchill and perhaps I could answer them more intelligently that way.

It might be a good thing to put them on the record and my hon. friend could look them up in the meantime. The first question is this: Did the Department of Railways and Canals carry on, direct, operations at Churchill during the summer of 1928, employing some eighty-five men or thereabouts, of whom twenty were superintendents and foremen, the others being workmen? And what was paid the foremen per hour, and how many hours per day did they work?
We have more men than that.

This is the summer of
1928.

While the information is being looked up, I may advise my hon. friend that last summer's work consisted very largely in getting ready for the actual work of this year. Some fifteen thousand tons of cargo were taken in and unloaded, temporary piers were built, temporary tracks laid, two dredges taken in, bunkhouses built, and a lot of work of that character done. As I said a moment ago, a doctor is there appointed by the department to look after the men, and there is a limited hospital accommodation.

What was the doctor's
name?
The total number of men at Churchill last year was three hundred and thirty-six.
That is the whole time, including the summer.
In 1928, yes. The numbers by months were: February, 17;. March, 30; April, 62; June, 227, making a total of 336.

How many stayed on
the work?

They practically all
stayed until the work was curtailed, and the staff put on a winter basis.

When was the work
closed down?

Our last boat last year
left Churchill about October 15 and there was a progressive reduction from that point on as the men could be taken out.

What was labourer's
pay?
Forty to forty-five cents per hour.
How many hours a day?

Time and a quarter for
time over ten hours and Sunday time.
Time and a quarter?
Yes.
And what did the foremen get?

Foremen-labourer, does
my hon. friend mean?
There were both superintendents and foremen; what did they get?

There are different kinds
of foremen. Does my hon. friend mean the foreman-1 abourer?
That will do for one.

Foreman-labourer, fifty
to eighty cents an hour.
Anything for overtime?

The same arrangement
for overtime; over ten hours, time and a quarter.

And board was paid for
at the rate of $1 per day? Who ran the boarding house?

It was part of the organization.

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
Who was the doctor in charge?
Doctor Walton.
What did he receive in the way of pay? Was there a fixed deduction from the men's wages?

He received $250 a
month and board.

Did the employment of
the men commence at The Pas?
For a time, yes.

Were any of those men
who went to Fort Churchill rejected because of medical unfitness at Fort Churohill and paid from the time they left The Pas until they returned?
The engineer advises me that there was only one such man.
Only one?
Yes.

Was there a man taken
on at Tisdale, subsequently rejected at Churchill and sent back at a cost to the country of $75 or $80?

The engineer in charge
states that he can remember only one such case and it does not come to his mind where the man was sent from. He was sent out with the idea that it was cheaper to do so than to keep him in the hospital there.
Was there a man named Scott employed as a carpenter on the recommendation of Curtin and Grant, barristers, Regina?
My hon. friend might ask some of his own friends about the letters they sent me and the endeavours which were made to get men employed.
I am not dealing with the minister himself but with Curtin and Grant of Regina.

As far as I know Curtin and Grant of Regina had mo power in the matter at all. Mr. Curtin is a friend of mine; I know him very well a,nd he has recommended men to me on various occasions, but not as a barrister or anything like that. With regard to the man named Scott, what is it my hon. friend wants to know?
Was there a man named Scott who was sent up as a carpenter at 75 cents an hour? According to my information he did not know a crosscut saw from a rip saw.
My hon. friend mentioned Scott previously this session. There were four Scotts there, working at different occupations.
This man was employed as a carpenter at 75 cents an hour.
There was a Scott who was a carpenter.
Classified as such?
Yes, classified as such and working as such.
It is said that he did not know the difference between a jig saw and a rip saw.

Can my hon. friend
make that statement on his own responsibility?

No. I am getting enough, much more than I expected. Then there was a man named Don Collins-inot John-a former druggist and a brother of Matt Collins of the Saskatchewan Liquor Board Was he employed; how long was he there; how long did he stay and what did he get? He was taken in to drive an engine at 85 cents an hour.
Is my hon. friend making that statement?
I am asking questions.

My hon. friend is putting statements on record and I want him to be fair to me in these matters. Inasmuch as my hon. friend is reading constantly from a document I am beginning to think I have a right to ask for that document.
You can keep on beginning, because you are not going to get it.

I think someone should
take responsibility for some of the statements my hon. friend is making. I am willing to answer questions.
Then suppose you do so. If the minister would answer questions he would advance the work of this committee. I asked if there was a man named Don Collins employed as an engineer at 85 cents an hour.

Then my hon. friend
went on to make a lot of statements about the Saskatchewan Liquor Board and so an.

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

I said he was a brother
of Matt Collins of the Saskatchewan Liquor Board.

I do not know that
there is a Matt Collins on the Saskatchewan Liquor Board.
I did not say you did.
The engineer informs me that there were two Collinses, one of whom was an engineer and the other a timekeeper. Be is not sure which one of them was Don.

Does he not know their
initials?
We have not the list of employees here. Has my hon. friend any criticism to make with regard to the employment of these two men? I am asking for my own information.

I will deal with that when the time comes. I am asking questions of the minister now; his estimates are before us. The public money is being spent and I am inquiring as to how it was spent. Now I want to know if a man called Buck Freeman was hired; if so, was he hired by a man named Miller of Ottawa, again on the recommendation of Curtin and Grant?
Is my hon. friend asking questions or making statements?
The minister knows exactly what I am doing.

My hon. friend should
be fairer to me than that.

I will put the question
again. Was there a man named Buck Freeman taken to Churchill as a carpenter at 75 cents an hour; was he hired by a man named Miller, of Ottawa; was that done on the recommendation of Curtin and Grant; what was his physical condition when he went to Churchill?
The engineer cannot recall any such circumstances as those related by my hon. friend. I know nothing of the matter myself.

How many storekeepers
were employed?

When the committee rose I was asking the minister a question with respect lo the employment of two or three persons named; I wanted to know whether or not he could locate them.
Mr. DUNNING': Donald Joseph Collins was an engineer operating the dinky locomotive. His rate of pay was 65 cents per hour and the hours worked were June, 30; July, 336i; August, 351; September, 338 and October, 372i.
At sixty-five cents per hour?
''Yes, with time and a quarter for over ten hours whenever more than ten hours were worked in one day.
The next was Buck Freeman.

If the man in question was Charles Freeman, who apparently was the only Freeman we had, he came in as a carpenter at 75 cents per hour and on August 1 was disrated to the status of a labourer and reduced to 45 cents per hour, and he continued in that capacity until October. The number of hours worked were June, 30; July, 340; August, 293; September, 289 and October, 291. From August 1 he was paid 45 cents per hour and prior to that time he received 75 cents.

On January 16 of this year, Mr. G. G. McGeer, on behalf of the council of the United Farmers of British Columbia, presented an appeal by way of a petition to the privy council, which in this case is the .cabinet, against certain rates from the prairies to the coast. I am not going to start at this day and date to argue the whole question; I desire only to indicate briefly the situation and ask the minister when a decision" is likely to be given. The question at issue is the dis-7S594-199J
criminatory rates allowed on wheat for export going from the prairies to British Columbia, as compared with the rates on wheat of an inferior grade for domestic consumption. The export wheat is generally numbers 1, 2 and 3, while the domestic wheat used for poultry feed is generally numbers 5 and 6, yet the more valuable wheat takes a rate less than half the rate charged for the inferior grade. The rate on export wheat from a central point of the prairies to Vancouver is 21 cents per hundred, and the rate on wheat for domestic use in British Columbia, taken out under identically the same conditions, is 41^ cents; a very heavy discrimination. It was brought out in the argument that Alberta grain could be landed in Yokohama for 50 cents a ton less than the same grain could be landed in Vancouver for domestic use. It would seem more profitable for our poultrymen to migrate to China and raise their eggs there and ship them to Canada. It was Shown that the difference in rates amounted to something like 81,000,000 a year to our British Columbia poultrymen. The cry is being raised for protection against eggs coming in from the United States and China, but here is a method which can be used, without raising the bogey of a tariff, which would give very substantial relief. The Minister of Railways will probably offer the time-honoured argument that export rates throughout the world always take a lower rating. I do not think that that argument will apply in this case, because there is no competing water route. In most cases where a lower export rate is quoted it is generally quoted in connection with water competition in whole or part, but there is no such thing as water competition between Calgary and Vancouver. Even allowing that the export rates should be lower-I do not allow that proposition, and the argument of Mr. McGeer does not allow it; in fact, he argues against it quite successfully, I think- than the rates for domestic use, I would point out that perhaps ten years ago there was a certain spread between the two rates. But in the course of time, through the application of various legislative enactments, the export rate has been reduced but the spread was not reduced accordingly. The export rate was reduced again but the spread still increases. Assuming that the spread between the export rate and the domestic rate ten years ago, was just and fair, Which I do not agree to, it cannot be just and fair to-day, because that spread has been increasing. As each successive decrease in the export rate was made no appropriate and corresponding reduction was made in the domestic rate, so

that to-day the spread between the two rates is something like double wihat it was a few years ago.	.

I wish to submit, on a

One of the anomalies of
our present system is that after the Board of Railway Commissioners has dealt with a matter there is an appeal to the governor general in council, that is the privy council, which is a political tribunal. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will recall that one of the leading journals of western Canada a few months ago pointed out that in the end this meant that governments must accept re-

sponsibility in connection with even matters of freight rates, although a tribunal was appointed that heard the case in the first instance. I said to my hon. friend from Vancouver South, who has been retained to act in this matter, that clearly no answer could be given by the Minister of Railways in connection with it because he could not give an answer on an ex parte statement by the hon. member himself, and to involve us in an argument would probably take longer time than the hon. gentleman would care to give to the question. But we have the anomaly that while there is an appeal on a question of law under certain circumstances to the Supreme Court of Canada, there is an appeal on questions of fact to the privy council which is a political body, and that involves, it seems to me, with all due deference, a prohibition against the minister giving answers to questions that are asked in the House of Commons touching matters that must be considered by him and his colleagues who must give judgment after hearing all parties concerned.

Before we dispose of this item, I had intended to ask the minister some questions with respect to the item of civil government and particularly with reference to 1he salary of the deputy minister. I was under the impression the civil government item had not passed. I think the house is entitled to a statement in this regard in view of the dual position which the deputy minister occupies as a director of the Canadian National railway system and Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals. The position is somewhat anomalous and may lead hereafter to some difficulties. I think it is not an unfair request that the minister should make a statement to the committee.

The item being passed, I do not wish to revert to it, but I will make a brief statement of the position. The house, of course, is aware of the serious loss which the department and the service of the country suffered in the death of the late deputy minister, Major Graham Bell, who had been a servant of Canada for more than thirty-eight years in various capacities, rising to Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals and a director of the Canadian National Railways. The problem of replacing Major Bell was a very difficult one. After casting around, the government determined on the appointment of the present deputy minister, Mr. R. A. C.
Henry, who had had a number of years' experience in the department and who, since reorganization, had been in the service of the Canadian National Railways as Director of the Bureau of Economics. I think all will acknowledge that Mr. Henry is eminently qualified in every way to serve. Frankly. I do not think I need enlarge upon the difficulty of securing, at the salary usually available for a deputy minister, the services of a man of the type required, who has to deal day by day with the high officers of the two great railway corporations. After the problem had been considered, it was decided to appoint Mr. Henry to the position at the salary usually accorded a deputy minister, to appoint him director of the Canadian National Railways, as his predecessor, Major Bell, had previously been, and, in addition, to take a few months of actual experience in the work to find out what extent the Canadian National Railways might properly be charged with a portion of his salary in respect to the services rendered as director of that institution. When I say a portion of his salary, I mean the enlargement of his salary beyond the amount ordinarily paid to a deputy minister. The committee will understand the problem when I say that Mr. Henry was receiving as Director of Economics of the Canadian National Railways more than half as much again as a deputy minister's salary. It is one of those difficulties which arise in connection with departments of this type dealing with such large affairs and requiring of its deputy minister a degree of ability and experience which the customary salary, as allowed by parliament, will not command. That is the difficulty, and I may tell the leader of the opposition that, as to the ultimate arrangement, nothing definite can be said to be settled. It was highly important that a capable and efficient deputy minister should be appointed. That was the first essential to keep the service operating and I am sure all who know Mr. Henry will applaud his selection, which I recommended to the government from the point of view of efficiency, ability and knowledge required. I am hoping that we shall succeed in making arrangements to retain Mr. Henry's services permanently. The problem had to be met immediately, and while I appreciate fully the difficulties involved, the solution arrived at is, I think, the best possible having regard to all the circumstances.

The situation is obviously an embarrassing one to deal with. I have heard nothing but the highest recommendation and commendation of the gentleman in

Supply-Railways and Canals
question. But apart altogether from the National Railway and leaving out the Canadian Pacific, it must be remembered that we have in Canada the Michigan Central railway, the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo railway, and one or two other independent lines, the first named being the most important of them. The difficulty is that under the act the Department of Railways and Canals and the deputy minister must deal with problems of very great importance affecting sometimes questions that intimately concern the operations of the road of which the deputy minister is a director-, and it is not right to ask the gentleman to assume responsibility as a director, and then act in a judicial capacity in establishing relations between his company and other companies under the act in question. The position with Mr. Bell was entirely different. He was merely a nominal director of the Canadian Northern acting as a liaison officer between the government and the railway. The present incumbent oacupied a position of great importance with the railway company and has now assumed the position of deputy minister, and it is very difficult to divorce a lifelong association with the railway company from one's duties in a new capacity. Until 1911, during a number of the formative 3'ears of my life, I was associated with a railway company, and for many years afterwards I found it exceedingly difficult to approach problems with that free and disinterested mind which is absolutely essential for the oondudt of business. I merely mention that because it does appear to me that the difficulty is much greater than the minister has indicated. There are very serious problems with which the deputy minister has to deal, and there are unconscious influences that shade and temper one's judgment, as I learned in my own life during a period of five or six years after I divorced myself from my previous employment with a railway company. That is a fact that cannot be lightly disregarded. I mention it because I think it is in the public interest that it should be mentioned. It is not a pleasant thing to refer to on the floor of the house, but the minister must realize that in the conduct of public business there are duties cast on those who sit to the left of the Speaker which are not pleasant but which must be discharged if it is not fairly to be said that they are derelict to the duties devolving upon them.

These further remarks
move me to say that both the minister and the deputy minister of railways are in a somewhat anomalous position in view of the present railway situation in Canada. Under

the Railway Act of Canada 'the minister and also the deputy minister have a definite statutory relationship and responsibility with respect to all the railways of Canada, but with respect to the Canadian National railway the minister occupies the position of representing the proprietors. He is, of course, for. that reason open-I will not say to the suspicion-but to conjecture that he might be inclined to favour the Canadian National system. In my capacity as Minister of Railways I have tried to be as judicial as one humanly can, and the deputy minister is just as capable, if not more capable than myself, of absolute fairness in these matters. But there is this to be remembered, which will be of some comfort to the hon. leader of the opposition, and I am sure he knows it already: that since the institution of the Board of Railway Commissioners the major part of what might be called the judicial functions of the minister and the deputy minister as between the different railways has been transferred to the 'board.
Not wholly.

Not wholly; because it is impossible to transfer them wholly, but certainly that anomalous position has been lessened by recent developments. I make no complaint over the question being raised by my hon. friend. I deem it of vital importance to the conduct of the Department of Railways and Canals that I should secure as deputy a man having the experience, training and ability, beyond all question, to deal with all phases of the department's work, and I am satisfied that in Mr. Henry I have such a man.

Would it not be desirable that the country Should pay him a salary commensurate with his work on the principle enunciated in connection with the post office workers that the labourer is worthy of his hire? The deputy minister, with the best intentions in the world, sits at the board and arrives at a conclusion with respect to a matter of policy that greatly affects the interests of one or two or three of the other railways in this country. He must then give effect to that policy in his capacity as deputy minister so far as the Department of Railways and Canals is concerned with administration in connection with that policy, and it is placing upon him a burden that is very difficult. He has to make invidious distinctions which, although I think he is a very highly trained officer, he must at times And it a little difficult to make. An ordinary person such as myself found that difficulty very

Supply-Railways and Canals
acute from 1911 to 1916. I should like to see the country pay a sum for such services as would gratify the wish of the minister that he should have about him a deputy upon whose judgment, knowledge and ability he can with confidence rely.

The situation in that regard is, as I indicated, still unsettled. I shall bear in mind my hon. friend's observations, although I would point out that if we once concede, as I think we must, that Canada's tremendous railway interests demand that the Deputy Minister of Railways should be a man capable of acting at least as vice-president of a railway corporation,, then the magnitude of the problem from the point of view of adequate remuneration becomes apparent. I shall not discuss it further exceipt to thank hon. members opposite for the manner in which they have referred to the matter.
Does this department have control over the right of way of steamships passing through the canals?
Yes. We control the flow of traffic through the canals.

Then I have three complaints which I would like to bring to the minister's notice. I tried to bring them up last year, but no action was taken. First, certain boats have right of way over all others. Second, there is the right of way that is given to what is known as package freighters, but there is a complaint that this right of way is given to package freighters carrying non-perishable fruit and that any boat not classed as such, when it comes to the entrance of the canal, may have to wait some hours till these other boats go through. The third complaint is that two American boats known as the Twin Ports and Twin Cities ran all last summer with right of way in Canadian canals which was not granted them in their own American canals. This right of way was given to the Twin Ports and the Twin Cities over the steamship Keystate. The complaint says that all last year and this year these tiwo boats have been given the right of way. They are a faster boat and the same right of way is not given them over their own American canals.

I remember my hon.
friend raising the matter a year ago, and I am not sure that I then read the regulation. So far as the three boats which he mentions are concerned, it is a question of which class they fall into under the regulations. I will read regulation 24 which relates to priority of passing through locks:
As regards priority of passage through the canals or locks, the following shall be the order of precedence:-
1.	Any government vessel.
2.	Vessels built and navigated for the express
purposes of the passenger traffic, running on schedule time; also excursion steamers and market boats.	_
3.	Vessels carrying general merchandise or package freight running on schedule time and talcing on, or delivering freight at local ports en route.
4.	Vessels built and navigated for the express purpose of freight traffic, even though carrying passengers to some limited extent; also private pleasure boats, yachts, skiffs, canoes, etc.
In the case of a vessel of the first or second class, above-mentioned, approaching a lock and being within such distance that She would be seriously or unduly delayed if any other boat lying in the tier and over which she has precedence were passed through before her, the lock shall be held for her accommodation.
Any violation or attempt to _ violate these provisions of precedence shall subject the owner or person in charge of the offending vessef to a penalty of not less than five dollars, and not exceeding one hundred dollars.
I shall be glad, to have the cases referred to looked into again.

I would like to
read this, because I asked the complainant to give it to me in writing. Last year he gave me the complaint that they arrived at the canal some hours before and yet had to wait there simply because these other two boats had sent a message ahead' that they were on their way. This is the complaint:
First, there are several Canadian boats which are listed as package freighters, but carry non-iperiishable goods such as iron, pipes, etc. westbound, and grain cargoes on the return trip. These vessels do not run on schedule yet they are being given the right of way, and due to the congestion in the canals we are compelled to wait from ten to twelve hours to enter the locks and then permit these boats to go ahead of us. Whereas a light ship requires only about twelve hours to pass through the canals these others take approximately twenty-four hours. At present there are a large number of boats which have a just claim for the right of way, and we are therefore delayed enough by these.
My second complaint is regarding the movement last year of two American boats, the Twin Ports and Twin Cities. These vessels were refused the right of way in American canals but still were given the preference over Canadian boats in Canadian canals.
In the third place I would like to refer to conditions at the west entrance to the Cornwall canal, Dickinson's landing. In previous years there was a float there which enabled boats to enter the lock in safety but it has been removed: and due to the current caused by the flow of water used for power purposes, the approach to the canal is now dangerous.

With respect to the
Cornwall canal, the last matter which he mentions, the improvement necessary there has been undertaken and is now practically

Supply-Railways and Canals
complete. With respect to the former matters I shall be glad, this being a matter of record, to have them carefully investigated.
The reason I read this was so that it would be on Hansard. This is from the captain of the steamship Keystate. He feels that his complaint is fair.

This is the same vote as last year. Mr. Weller entered the service of the department in 1883 as an engineer in canal construction and operation. In 1900 he was appointed superintending engineer of the Welland canal, which office he held till 1912 when he was appointed engineer in charge of survey and design of construction of the then proposed new Welland ship canal. He remained in charge of the work till 1917, when it was closed down owing to the war, and his services were dispensed with. From January, 1919, to March, 1927, the services of Mr. Weller were retained in a consulting capacity because of his early connection with the development of the Welland canal plans. He is now retired, and in view of his services it was thought that $3,500 was not an unreasonable allowance to make. He is a very old man and has no other pension rights whatever.

I desire to state with regard to the pictures to which my hon. friend from Vancouver-ilurrard, the hon. member for Kingston and the member for Muskoka referred, that I had hoped last night before the discussion ended to be able to give them the information they asked for. Some of the staff got in touch with the director and asked

All he can say is, they

He cannot say even that
without checking it up. However, he gave me a statement this morning with regard to the three pictures referred to. I 'have the following memorandum with regard to these portraits:
Lord Byng: This portrait by John Sargent belongs to the national gallery collection and not the Canadian war memorials and was purchased in 1925 from the national gallery vote. It has been hanging in the collection ever since and is hanging now on floor No. 2.
General Currie: This portrait by Orpen belongs to the Canadian war memorials collection. It has hung temporarily in the national gallery at various times and is at present on loan to His Excellency the Governor General, at government house.
General Lipsett: This portrait, also by Orpen, belongs to the Canadian %var memorials. It has been exhibited temporarily in the national gallery at various times.
It was withdrawn first for loan, at the urgent request of the commandant, to the Royal Military College, Kingston.
Later it was again lent to Sir William Orpen for the purpose of making a replica for presentation to General Lipsett's native^ town. Merthyr Tydfil, at the request of that city. It has now been returned and. pending the usual rearrangement of the exhibition in the national gallery it is being kept with the rest of the Canadian war memorials collection in the new fireproof storage space in the auditorium building.
Since what date has the Sargent picture been hanging?
Since it was purchased.

I made a very careful
search a few weeks ago and asked1 particularly for it but I could not find it.

I have given my hon.
friend the statement submitted to me by the director and I take it to be correct.

What jurisdiction has the
director of the gallery over the war memorial pictures?

The national gallery has
been the custodian of the Canadian war memorials since 1919. The national gallery has exhibited them temporarily twice and
they have also been exhibited twice in Montreal and Toronto during that time. The whole collection consists of 360 paintings and sculptures and prints, and it would be impossible to exhibit them permanently in the national gallery for want of space. The national gallery, out of its own fund, has paid for necessary restoration work and upon its representations to the government last year, better and more perfectly fireproof storage was secured for them in the auditorium building. The collection is there now waiting for the building of a new national gallery which it is expected will include a special wing devoted to them. The trustees of the national gallery have never ceased to urge in every annual report and through every other possible means the necessity of providing a permanent and public home for the Canadian war memorials.
What proportion of this year's vote	will be	expended	on new	pictures?
The sum of $85,000.

Does the minister think
he is justified in purchasing new pictures when we have nowhere to hang them?

These picutres that are
being purchased are by noted artists and include what are considered by the trustees of the gallery to be works of special merit which they	should	obtain. Not only	arethey exhibited in the gallery, as far as it is possible to	display	them, but part of	thescheme is	to lend	them to	various local
organizations from one end of the country to the other. They are kept on exhibition practically all the time in one place or another.

I cannot possibly understand why these war memorial pictures should be locked up in basements. Why is it necessary that portraits of men like General Lipsett should be stored in some basement in the city of Ottawa? Why should not such a portrait be hanging in the gallery? From personal observation I know that there are in the gallery things which I at any rate consider absurdities when compared with such portraits. If the minister will visit the gallery he will see there pictures of ducks and bunches of roses and geese and numerous landscape scenes, as well as George Washington, who, it is true, was a great character and all that. But why should there not be some portraits of our own national characters? I cannot understand a policy that excludes from the gallery the portraits of men who have made history for our country, while
